title: Coronary Artery Disease: Separate Acute Ischemia From Chronic Risk Management
bottomLine: Coronary artery disease care starts by deciding whether symptoms represent possible acute coronary syndrome. Once acute ischemia is excluded, management is risk-based: smoking cessation, lipid lowering, BP/diabetes control, antiplatelet therapy when indicated, antianginal treatment and referral/testing matched to symptom burden and pretest probability.
recognize: Exertional pressure, heaviness, dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance can represent chronic ischemia even without classic central chest pain.
New rest pain, accelerating frequency, prolonged symptoms or associated instability shifts the pathway to ACS evaluation.
differentiate: Musculoskeletal, reflux, pulmonary and anxiety symptoms can mimic CAD; the clinical pattern and cardiovascular risk modify pretest probability.
A normal resting ECG does not exclude chronic coronary disease.
assessment: Characterize symptom trigger/duration/relief, prior vascular disease, smoking, BP, diabetes, kidney disease, family history, medications and bleeding risk.
Assess whether the patient can exercise and whether baseline ECG/comorbidity affects test selection.
workup: Use ECG and evidence-based noninvasive testing selected by pretest probability, ability to exercise and local access; avoid routine testing when probability is very low and no red flags exist.
Escalate to acute biomarkers/imaging when ACS cannot be excluded.
management: Use secondary-prevention therapy for established ASCVD and health-behaviour modification for all.
Treat angina with evidence-based antianginal therapy and refer for cardiology/revascularization assessment when symptoms persist, diagnosis is uncertain or high-risk anatomy is suspected.
Address cardiac rehabilitation and risk-factor control after prior MI/revascularization.
medicationSafety: Antiplatelet therapy requires indication and bleeding-risk review rather than automatic use in every chest-pain patient.
Nitrates can cause hypotension and are unsafe with recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure.
counselling: Teach which symptom changes require emergency evaluation rather than routine follow-up.
Frame lipid/BP/smoking treatment as risk reduction rather than punishment for a laboratory number.
followUp: Track symptoms/function, adherence/tolerance and completion of ordered diagnostic/referral pathways.
examTrap: Calling recurrent rest pain 'stable CAD' because the patient already has a coronary diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: Chronic CAD management begins only after acute ischemia is reasonably excluded.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society secondary-prevention/chronic coronary resources

title: Heart Failure Across EF: Congestion, Perfusion, Phenotype, and Foundational Therapy
bottomLine: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome, not an EF label. First distinguish congestion from low-output instability and identify the precipitant; then classify EF/phenotype and use disease-modifying therapy supported for that phenotype while treating comorbidities and volume status.
recognize: Orthopnea, PND, edema, elevated JVP, crackles and rapid weight gain support congestion; cool extremities, hypotension, oliguria and altered mentation suggest poor perfusion.
HF with EF >40% remains heart failure when signs/symptoms and objective cardiac dysfunction/congestion are present; normal EF does not mean normal cardiac function.
differentiate: BNP/NT-proBNP supports but does not diagnose HF alone and is influenced by age, AF, kidney disease and obesity.
Edema/dyspnea can come from renal, hepatic, venous, pulmonary or deconditioning causes.
assessment: Assess volume, perfusion, BP, rhythm, oxygenation, renal function, precipitating ischemia/infection/arrhythmia, medication adherence and drugs such as NSAIDs.
Review frailty, kidney disease, diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea, iron deficiency and goals of care.
workup: Use ECG, renal function/electrolytes, CBC and cause-directed tests plus echocardiography to define structure/EF.
Consider natriuretic peptide and ischemic/rhythm evaluation when they will change management.
management: For HFrEF, use foundational disease-modifying therapy across ARNI/RAAS inhibition, evidence-based beta blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor when suitable; use diuretics for congestion.
For symptomatic HF with non-reduced EF, follow the current 2025 CCS/CHFS HFnrEF recommendations, including therapies supported for the phenotype and aggressive treatment of comorbidities/congestion.
Escalate pulmonary edema, shock, severe renal injury or poor perfusion to acute care.
medicationSafety: Monitor BP, renal function and potassium during RAAS/ARNI/MRA titration.
Do not initiate/aggressively titrate beta blockers during cardiogenic shock or severe unstable decompensation.
SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/peri-procedural counselling and ketoacidosis awareness.
counselling: Teach daily symptom/weight awareness where useful, sodium/fluid advice individualized to the patient, and when to seek urgent care.
Explain that feeling less congested after diuresis does not replace disease-modifying therapy.
followUp: Reassess after medication changes for BP, renal function/electrolytes, congestion and tolerance; close the loop on cardiology and rehabilitation referrals.
examTrap: Treating preserved EF as 'not heart failure' or using diuretics alone in HFrEF without foundational therapy.
oneLinePearl: Treat the syndrome first, then treat the EF phenotype with evidence-based therapy.

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Stability, Stroke Prevention, Then Rate vs Rhythm Strategy
bottomLine: Atrial fibrillation management has three separate questions: is the patient unstable, does the patient need stroke prevention, and is rate control or rhythm control the better symptom/outcome strategy? Do not let a successful rate-control decision answer the anticoagulation question.
recognize: AF causes an irregular atrial rhythm and may present with palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, HF or be asymptomatic.
Hemodynamic instability, ongoing ischemia or acute pulmonary edema changes the pathway to urgent synchronized cardioversion.
differentiate: Rate control controls ventricular response but does not restore sinus rhythm; rhythm control includes cardioversion and antiarrhythmic/ablation strategies.
Stroke-prevention decisions depend on validated Canadian risk assessment and patient factors, not symptom severity.
assessment: Assess onset/duration, hemodynamics, HF/ischemia, prior stroke/TIA, hypertension, diabetes, age, renal function, bleeding history, thyroid disease, alcohol and sleep apnea.
Confirm current anticoagulant/last dose if cardioversion is possible.
workup: Use ECG for diagnosis and targeted thyroid/electrolyte/echo evaluation based on context.
For elective cardioversion, thromboembolic risk and AF duration determine anticoagulation/TEE strategy through the current guideline pathway.
management: Use rate control when appropriate for symptoms/physiology and rhythm control when symptoms, early disease, HF or other patient factors support it.
Use CCS/CHRS stroke-prevention guidance independently of rate/rhythm choice.
Refer for electrophysiology/ablation consideration when recurrent symptomatic AF persists despite appropriate strategy or patient preference supports it.
medicationSafety: Rate-slowing drugs can worsen bradycardia/hypotension and require HF/conduction context.
Antiarrhythmic selection depends on structural heart disease, renal/hepatic function, QT/conduction and interactions.
Anticoagulants require renal function, bleeding risk and interaction review.
counselling: Explain that AF symptom control and stroke prevention are different treatment goals.
Address alcohol, sleep apnea, weight/BP and other modifiable risk factors.
followUp: Track symptoms, rate/rhythm, anticoagulation adherence/tolerance and renal function; revisit rhythm strategy if burden persists.
examTrap: Stopping anticoagulation because sinus rhythm was restored or because the ventricular rate is well controlled.
oneLinePearl: AF has three decisions: stability, stroke prevention, and rate-versus-rhythm strategy.
sourceBasis: 2020 Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society AF guideline

title: Stable Angina: Stable Only When the Pattern Is Stable
bottomLine: Stable angina is a reproducible exertional ischemic syndrome without a new unstable pattern. Confirm that the symptoms are truly stable, estimate coronary probability, choose appropriate noninvasive testing when needed, then combine antianginal therapy with secondary prevention.
recognize: Predictable exertional chest pressure or ischemic equivalent that improves with rest/antianginal therapy can fit stable angina.
Rest pain, increasing frequency/severity, prolonged symptoms or reduced threshold are unstable features until proven otherwise.
differentiate: Reflux, chest wall pain and dyspnea from lung disease can mimic angina.
A normal resting ECG does not exclude inducible ischemia.
assessment: Characterize trigger/relief/duration, exercise tolerance, prior CAD/revascularization, risk factors, BP, anemia/thyroid contributors and medication adherence.
Assess nitrate/PDE-5 exposure and baseline bradycardia/hypotension before antianginal changes.
workup: Use ECG and appropriate stress/anatomic testing matched to probability, exercise capacity, baseline ECG and local availability.
Do not delay ACS evaluation when the pattern is not truly stable.
management: Use antianginal therapy tailored to HR/BP/comorbidity plus antiplatelet/lipid/BP/diabetes secondary prevention when indicated.
Refer for cardiology/revascularization when symptoms remain limiting despite therapy or high-risk anatomy/ischemia is suspected.
medicationSafety: Nitrates can cause hypotension and are contraindicated with recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure.
Beta blockers/non-DHP calcium-channel blockers require bradycardia/conduction/HF context.
counselling: Teach when a familiar angina pattern has changed enough to require emergency care.
Reinforce cardiac rehabilitation/activity plan and smoking cessation.
followUp: Track functional limitation, medication tolerance and completion of planned diagnostic/cardiology review.
examTrap: Calling new rest pain stable because the patient has a history of exertional angina.
oneLinePearl: Stable angina is stable only if the trigger, severity and relief pattern remain stable.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society chronic coronary/secondary-prevention resources

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome: ECG, Serial Troponin, Reperfusion and Bleeding Risk
bottomLine: Suspected ACS is time-sensitive. Obtain ECG promptly, use serial high-sensitivity troponin in the validated local pathway, identify STEMI/reperfusion needs and treat ischemia/antithrombotic risk while also considering lethal alternatives such as aortic dissection and PE.
recognize: Pressure/heaviness, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue or epigastric discomfort can be ischemic presentations.
Women, older adults and people with diabetes may present without classic chest pain.
differentiate: STEMI requires rapid reperfusion; NSTEMI/unstable presentations use serial ECG/troponin and risk stratification.
Aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax and pericarditis can mimic ACS and alter antithrombotic safety.
assessment: Assess ABCs, hemodynamics, symptom onset, bleeding risk, anticoagulants, recent surgery, stimulant use and aortic/PE clues.
Check oxygenation rather than applying routine oxygen to every chest-pain patient.
workup: Obtain 12-lead ECG urgently and repeat with evolving symptoms; use serial high-sensitivity troponin according to the validated local algorithm.
Use additional imaging/testing based on alternate diagnoses and complications.
management: Activate regional STEMI reperfusion pathways without outpatient delay.
Use guideline-directed antiplatelet/anticoagulant/anti-ischemic therapy according to diagnosis and bleeding risk after checking contraindications.
Treat shock, HF or malignant arrhythmia in monitored acute care.
medicationSafety: Do not give fibrinolysis when aortic dissection is suspected.
Nitrates can worsen hypotension and are unsafe after recent PDE-5 inhibitors.
Avoid reflex oxygen in normoxemia.
counselling: Explain why improvement or one normal early test does not necessarily exclude ACS.
followUp: After stabilization, ensure medication reconciliation, secondary prevention, cardiac rehabilitation and follow-up.
examTrap: Sending a concerning patient home after one normal early troponin or delaying STEMI transfer for outpatient testing.
oneLinePearl: ACS is a serial diagnosis and a time-to-treatment problem.

title: Valvular Heart Disease: Murmur Plus Symptoms Determines Urgency
bottomLine: A murmur is a clue, not a diagnosis. Symptoms, examination, echocardiographic severity and ventricular response determine referral urgency; exertional syncope, HF, new post-MI murmur or fever with a new murmur requires rapid escalation.
recognize: Aortic stenosis can cause exertional dyspnea, angina or syncope; mitral regurgitation can cause HF/AF symptoms.
Innocent murmurs occur, particularly in children/young adults, but should not have abnormal pulses, cyanosis, growth failure or exertional red flags.
differentiate: A new murmur with fever/bacteremia risk raises endocarditis; a new murmur after MI can indicate mechanical complication.
Murmur intensity does not perfectly correlate with severity, especially in low-output states.
assessment: Assess timing/location/radiation, BP/pulses, JVP, HF signs, exercise symptoms, syncope, AF and infection history.
Review prior echocardiograms and whether symptoms have changed.
workup: Order echocardiography when structural disease is suspected or symptoms/signs warrant it.
Use ECG and additional imaging/cardiology testing according to the confirmed lesion.
management: Refer moderate/severe symptomatic valve disease to cardiology/valve team and manage HF/AF complications while definitive intervention is planned.
Do not use antibiotics for dental prophylaxis in every murmur; prophylaxis is reserved for defined high-risk cardiac conditions.
medicationSafety: Avoid aggressive preload reduction in unstable severe fixed outflow obstruction without expert oversight.
Anticoagulation decisions in valve disease depend on rhythm/prosthesis/lesion context.
counselling: Teach the symptoms that signal progression and explain why surveillance intervals depend on lesion severity.
followUp: Ensure scheduled echo/cardiology surveillance and close the loop on new symptoms rather than waiting for the next routine scan.
examTrap: Giving dental antibiotic prophylaxis to every patient with a murmur—or reassuring exertional syncope because the murmur is not loud.
oneLinePearl: Valve disease risk is symptoms plus structure, not murmur volume alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular heart disease resources

title: Peripheral Artery Disease: Limb Symptoms Are a Cardiovascular Risk Signal
bottomLine: PAD is systemic atherosclerotic disease. Confirm suspected claudication with vascular examination and ABI/vascular testing when appropriate, aggressively manage cardiovascular risk, prescribe structured exercise and escalate acute limb ischemia or chronic limb-threatening ischemia urgently.
recognize: Exertional calf/thigh/buttock discomfort relieved by rest suggests claudication; rest pain, nonhealing wounds or gangrene indicate advanced ischemia.
PAD may be asymptomatic yet still signals high cardiovascular risk.
differentiate: Spinal stenosis, neuropathy and musculoskeletal pain can mimic claudication.
Acute limb ischemia is sudden pain/pallor/pulselessness/paresthesia/paralysis/poikilothermia and is a vascular emergency.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, pulses, skin/wounds, capillary refill, diabetes, smoking, CAD/stroke, renal disease and foot-care risks.
Check for noncompressible arteries in diabetes/CKD when ABI interpretation is atypical.
workup: Use ABI and vascular lab testing to support diagnosis; toe pressure/duplex or further imaging is used when ABI is unreliable or intervention is considered.
management: Use smoking cessation, lipid lowering, BP/diabetes management, antiplatelet therapy when indicated and supervised/structured exercise.
Refer lifestyle-limiting claudication despite optimized therapy and chronic limb-threatening ischemia to vascular care; acute limb ischemia requires emergency transfer.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic choice depends on vascular indication and bleeding risk; do not combine agents without a guideline-supported reason.
Foot wounds/infection in ischemic limbs can deteriorate rapidly and require multidisciplinary care.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive infection in ischemic foot
counselling: Frame walking/exercise therapy as treatment, not merely lifestyle advice; reinforce foot inspection and smoking cessation.
followUp: Track walking distance/function, wounds, pulses and cardiovascular-risk therapy; ensure vascular referrals are closed-loop.
examTrap: Treating claudication only as a leg problem while ignoring secondary cardiovascular prevention—or missing acute limb ischemia.
oneLinePearl: PAD is both a limb disease and a whole-body ASCVD diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Peripheral Arterial Disease resources

title: DVT and PE: Confirm Efficiently, Anticoagulate Deliberately, Reassess Duration
bottomLine: VTE management starts with validated diagnostic probability and then separates acute severity, anticoagulant choice and treatment duration. Do not use D-dimer as a diagnosis or assume every provoked/unprovoked event has the same long-term anticoagulation plan.
recognize: Unilateral swelling/pain supports DVT; dyspnea, pleuritic pain, syncope or hypoxemia can signal PE.
Cancer, surgery, immobilization, estrogen/pregnancy and prior VTE are important provoking factors.
differentiate: Cellulitis, Baker cyst and venous insufficiency can mimic DVT.
High-risk PE is hemodynamic; clot burden alone does not define severity.
assessment: Assess probability, hemodynamics, oxygenation, bleeding risk, pregnancy, cancer, renal/hepatic function, provoking factors and prior VTE.
Review interacting drugs and current anticoagulants.
workup: Use a validated DVT/PE diagnostic algorithm with D-dimer selectively and compression ultrasound/CTPA/VQ imaging according to probability/context.
For confirmed PE, assess severity/RV strain when it changes disposition.
management: Treat confirmed proximal DVT/PE with anticoagulation unless contraindicated; Thrombosis Canada recommends at least 3 months for DVT, then reassess duration based on provoking factors/recurrence/bleeding risk.
Use pregnancy-, cancer-, renal- and interaction-appropriate anticoagulants.
Escalate high-risk PE and limb-threatening DVT to specialist/acute-care pathways.
medicationSafety: DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding; pregnancy treatment uses LMWH in current Canadian guidance.
Warfarin/DOAC therapy requires interaction, renal function, bleeding and adherence review.
counselling: Teach bleeding precautions, adherence and symptoms of recurrence; explain why duration is revisited rather than automatically lifelong or always three months.
followUp: Reassess anticoagulation duration, renal function, bleeding and persistent dyspnea/post-thrombotic symptoms.
examTrap: Treating a positive D-dimer as confirmed VTE or stopping all VTE treatment automatically at three months without reviewing whether the event was unprovoked/high-risk.
oneLinePearl: VTE requires three decisions: diagnosis, acute severity, and anticoagulation duration.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada VTE Duration of Treatment guide (Apr 2026)

title: Dyslipidemia: Choose Lipid Therapy by Cardiovascular Risk, Not LDL Alone
bottomLine: Lipid therapy is risk-based. Separate secondary prevention and statin-indicated conditions from lower-risk primary prevention, then use maximally tolerated statin and evidence-based nonstatin therapy when guideline thresholds/clinical risk justify intensification.
recognize: Established ASCVD generally warrants intensive lipid lowering unless contraindicated or inconsistent with goals of care.
Diabetes, CKD, familial hypercholesterolemia/very high LDL and calculated risk can create treatment indications without prior ASCVD.
differentiate: A moderately high LDL in a low-risk patient is not automatically more urgent than a lower LDL in someone with established vascular disease.
Reported statin symptoms should be assessed for timing, interactions and alternate causes before permanent intolerance is declared.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, smoking, BP, diabetes, CKD, family history, pregnancy potential, medications/interactions and prior statin response.
Review secondary causes when the pattern is unexpected/severe.
workup: Use lipid profile and a Canadian risk framework for primary prevention when applicable; consider ApoB/non-HDL-C and other risk modifiers per CCS guidance.
CK/liver testing is targeted to symptoms/risk rather than routine repeated screening in every stable patient.
management: Use statin therapy according to prevention category and maximize tolerated intensity when risk supports it.
Add evidence-based nonstatin therapy when secondary-prevention/high-risk thresholds remain above recommended levels despite tolerated statin therapy.
Lifestyle intervention remains foundational.
medicationSafety: Review major statin interactions and investigate significant muscle weakness/dark urine or hepatotoxicity symptoms.
Pregnancy/planning pregnancy requires medication-specific review rather than routine continuation.
counselling: Explain absolute-risk reduction and expected benefit rather than presenting treatment as punishment for a number.
followUp: Repeat lipids after meaningful initiation/intensification to assess response/adherence, then at clinically appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Withholding indicated statin because LDL is not dramatically high in a patient with established ASCVD.
oneLinePearl: Treat vascular risk first; the lipid panel helps select and monitor the therapy.

title: Syncope: Identify Cardiac and Hemorrhagic Risk Before Calling It Vasovagal
bottomLine: Syncope is transient global cerebral hypoperfusion. The workup is driven by event history, ECG, orthostatic/cardiac findings and red flags—not routine neuroimaging; exertional syncope, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease or major bleeding requires urgent cardiac/acute-care evaluation.
recognize: Vasovagal syncope often has a trigger/prodrome and rapid recovery; orthostatic syncope follows postural volume/autonomic or medication context.
Cardiac syncope may be abrupt, exertional or occur with structural heart disease/abnormal ECG.
differentiate: Seizure usually has prolonged postictal confusion/stereotyped features; hypoglycemia/intoxication can mimic loss of consciousness.
Routine CT head has low value in uncomplicated syncope without trauma or focal neurologic signs.
assessment: Obtain patient/witness event description, orthostatic vitals when safe, cardiac/neurologic examination and medication/bleeding/pregnancy review.
Ask exertional trigger, palpitations, chest pain, family history sudden death and prior structural disease.
workup: ECG is core testing; glucose/pregnancy/CBC/electrolytes or rhythm monitoring are targeted to the clinical differential.
Use echocardiography, ambulatory monitoring or specialty testing when structural/arrhythmic disease is plausible rather than ordering a universal test panel.
management: Urgently evaluate cardiac/high-risk or hemorrhagic features.
Treat orthostatic/vasovagal causes with trigger, volume and medication strategies when appropriate.
Driving/work restrictions depend on cause/risk and provincial/CCS guidance.
medicationSafety: Antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha blockers, sedatives and QT-prolonging drugs can contribute; medication review is part of treatment.
counselling: Teach hydration/trigger strategies only after dangerous causes are reasonably excluded and provide driving/safety advice.
followUp: Close the loop on rhythm monitoring/cardiology referral when intermittent arrhythmia remains plausible.
examTrap: Ordering routine CT head for uncomplicated syncope while missing exertional history and an abnormal ECG.
oneLinePearl: Syncope evaluation is history + ECG + risk, not routine brain imaging.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada syncope imaging principles
